title: Part 1 — Mashq 1
textTemplate: For centuries, coffeehouses have served as more than places to drink coffee. In seventeenth-century London, they became known (1)___ "penny universities," because for the price of a single cup, a visitor could sit for hours listening to debates (2)___ politics, science, and literature. Merchants conducted business there, poets read their latest work, and strangers exchanged news long (3)___ newspapers became widely available. Some historians argue (4)___ the modern stock exchange has its roots in a London coffeehouse, where traders once gathered daily to discuss shipping prices. Although coffeehouses today rarely serve (5)___ centers of political debate the way they once did, many still function as informal meeting places (6)___ freelancers, students, and small business owners who cannot afford a private office.

texts.label: A
texts.title: GreenCart
texts.text: GreenCart delivers grocery orders within two hours in major Uzbek cities. The company initially struggled because customers doubted that fresh produce could survive fast delivery without quality loss. To address this, GreenCart introduced a public satisfaction guarantee: any customer unhappy with the freshness of their order receives an automatic refund, no questions asked. This policy, though costly at first, gradually rebuilt customer confidence and is now central to the brand's reputation.

texts.label: B
texts.title: PathFinder Logistics
texts.text: PathFinder Logistics specializes in moving oversized industrial equipment across difficult terrain. Unlike competitors who rely on standard trucking routes, the company invests heavily in route-planning software that maps out alternative paths around seasonal road closures. While this technology was expensive to develop, it has allowed PathFinder to guarantee delivery windows that rival companies consider impossible to promise.

texts.label: C
texts.title: Silk Thread Apparel
texts.text: Silk Thread Apparel manufactures traditional textiles using techniques passed down through several generations of the same family. The company deliberately avoids automating certain production steps, arguing that machine-made goods cannot replicate the subtle irregularities that customers associate with authentic handcraft. This decision limits how quickly the company can scale production, but has helped it command premium prices in export markets.

questions.statement: Which company deliberately limits its own growth potential in order to preserve a particular quality?
Which company had to overcome initial customer skepticism about its core service?
Which company relies on technology to achieve something competitors say cannot be done?
Which company offers a policy that removes financial risk for the customer?
Which company bases part of its value on techniques that are old rather than modern?

title: Part 3 — Mashq 1 (Matching Headings)
text:
Choosing a Career Path

15) Many young people feel pressured to decide on a career direction while still in their teens, long before they have any real experience of what different jobs actually involve day to day. This mismatch between early decision-making and limited experience is one reason career changes later in life are so common.

16) Career counsellors increasingly recommend short trial placements, sometimes just a few days long, before committing to a field of study. Even a brief taste of the daily reality of a job can reveal a mismatch that months of research never would.

17) Parents often mean well when they push their children toward stable, well-paying professions, but this advice can backfire when it ignores a young person's genuine interests. Employees who feel little connection to their chosen field frequently report lower job satisfaction, regardless of salary.

18) Some experts now argue that the idea of a single, lifelong career is becoming outdated. With industries changing rapidly, the ability to learn new skills may matter more than any specific early choice.

title: Part 4 — Mashq 1 (MC + True/False/No Info)
text:
A Second Chance for Old Furniture

Farrukh never planned to start a business repairing old furniture. It began as a hobby after he restored a broken chair he found near his apartment building, simply because he disliked seeing it go to waste. A neighbour who saw the finished chair offered to pay him to restore a table, and within a year, word of mouth had turned his hobby into a small workshop with a growing waiting list.

What surprised Farrukh most was not the demand itself, but who his customers were. He had expected mostly older clients holding onto sentimental family pieces, but instead, many of his customers were young professionals who preferred restoring a unique, well-made older piece to buying a mass-produced new one. Several told him they liked knowing the exact history of their furniture, something a factory-made item could never offer.
